title: You Turn the Page and Forget What You Know
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions, March 16, 2026
summary: Chiarelli explains the Gell-Mann Amnesia Effect: readers spot errors in articles about their expertise, then read unfamiliar topics with complete credulity, forgetting what they witnessed. LLMs are the perfect Gell-Mann machine, producing uniform fluency across all domains, triggering trust transfer even where underlying content is unsound. The author provides a five-step validation funnel: flag expertise boundaries, cross-check with second models, verify sources manually, audit logic and structure, and request expert spot-checks. The antidote is portable skepticism—treating observed error rates as a prior for everything else from that source.
points: LLMs produce surface features that trigger trust transfer uniformly across domains regardless of content accuracy.
Expertise is domain-specific and doesn't port across fields; credibility bleeds implicitly into adjacent domains.
AI fabricates citations with complete fluency, making manual verification of statistics, quotes, and studies essential.
Where two AI models confidently disagree, you have found claims that need in-depth verification.
Surface quality doesn't vary between sections the AI got right and wrong, making explicit QA critical.
quotes: You see the errors where you can spot them, and then proceed as if they're localised anomalies rather than evidence about the underlying quality of everything else.

Knowing the effect exists is the easy part. Knowing exactly where it applies to you is what matters.” “Your QA effort should increase in proportion to how far the content sits from your own expertise.
Those best placed to use these tools are the ones who have mapped, honestly, where their own knowledge runs out.” Archived from The Art of Asking Questions on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
